claims.text: The proposed intervention is addition of 1–2 wt% Hf to a NbMoTaW-based refractory high-entropy alloy.
The Hf-modified alloy will be subjected to sub-solidus annealing near 0.8Tm.
Annealing near 0.8Tm with optimized time-temperature parameters will cause Hf to segregate selectively to grain boundaries.
The proposed treatment can produce grain-boundary Hf segregation without forming deleterious secondary phases.
The initial NbMoTaW-based alloy has a homogeneous microstructure.
The initial alloy has limited ductility and is prone to brittle grain-boundary failure under dynamic loading.
Hf segregation modifies grain-boundary interfacial chemistry and reduces localized stress concentrations.
Reduced grain-boundary energy and stress concentration facilitate distributed grain-boundary sliding under load.
Distributed grain-boundary sliding improves ductility and plastic-deformation uniformity.
Selective grain-boundary segregation leaves the strength of the grain interiors uncompromised.
The treatment will not compromise the alloy's impact-induced stored-energy release mechanism.
Relative to the untreated baseline, the Hf-modified and annealed alloy will have significantly improved room-temperature ductility.
Relative to the untreated baseline, the treated alloy will exhibit more uniform deformation under dynamic loading.
The treated alloy will retain high yield strength.
The treated alloy will retain its capacity for impact-induced energy release.
The mechanical-property improvement depends on avoiding matrix depletion and secondary-phase precipitation or coarsening.
Departures from the required annealing time or temperature can compromise the balance between ductility and strength.
